## “Compound R significantly suppresses inflammation” {#r-lab-meeting .interaction}

<p class="small">Stimulated cultured cells were treated with vehicle or compound R.<br>Protein signal was quantified in triplicate.</p><img class="data-plot workshop-plot" src="figures/generated/workshop-opening.png" alt="Lab-meeting plot: three measurements each for vehicle and R, with mean bars." /><p class="takeaway">p = 0.032 &nbsp; · &nbsp; n = 3</p><p class="prompt-tag">Would you believe this conclusion?</p>

::: notes
**Time: 02:42–02:43 (1 minute).**

**Say:** Give participants one minute to react without correcting them. Present this as a colleague asking for help, not a trap or evidence of incompetence. The illustrative report omits information that participants must request. Do not lead with which test was used. Instructor-only provenance: this is Line B, day 2, P1, high dose versus stimulated vehicle. Three assay wells per condition are aliquots of one treated culture-tube lysate, not three independently treated cultures. Mean signals are 100 and 86.8169. The displayed Welch calculation on technical wells is exactly .032, but does not justify biological treatment inference. Do not reveal this yet. The entire workshop is fictional teaching data.

**Conceptual point:** A reported p-value and n do not define the evidence.

**Likely misconception:** The result must be either real or false based on the threshold.

**Optional follow-up:** What is your first reaction, and what would change it?

**Facilitation:** Participant reasoning takes priority over instructor explanation. Use these notes selectively; do not read them aloud. This is a fictional teaching scenario, not a published biological finding.
:::

## What do you need to know before interpreting this? {#r-information-first .interaction}

<p class="question">Ask the researcher.</p><p class="small">Collect questions before offering advice.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 02:43–02:46 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Let participants supply questions for roughly two minutes, then group them verbally for one minute. Do not display a checklist. If needed, ask one neutral follow-up. Listen for what n counts; independent repetition; culture/well generation; contemporaneous vehicle; allocation across days; line shown; proteins, doses and comparisons inspected; exclusion rationale; prospective hypothesis and analysis; population or experimental space. Answer that these details are available on the next slides. Reward requests for provenance without turning this into an exam. Avoid labelling exploratory work as misconduct.

**Conceptual point:** Seek information before judging or prescribing an analysis.

**Likely misconception:** The only missing detail is the name of the test.

**Optional follow-up:** What in the laboratory notebook would help you interpret n?

**Facilitation:** Participant reasoning takes priority over instructor explanation. Use these notes selectively; do not read them aloud. This is a fictional teaching scenario, not a published biological finding.
:::

## What was actually repeated? {#r-hierarchy .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Guess each layer before revealing</p>
<div class="workshop-hierarchy">
<p class="fragment">Two cell lines → one newly initiated preparation per line per day</p>
<p class="fragment">Each preparation → available vehicle / low / medium / high dose tubes</p>
<p class="fragment">One treated tube per available condition → one lysate</p>
<p class="fragment">Each lysate → three assay wells → five protein measurements</p></div>
<p class="takeaway">What is the experimental unit? What does n = 3 count?</p>

::: notes
**Time: 02:46–02:47 (1 minute).**

**Say:** Reveal each layer after asking for a guess. There are two established cell lines, three experiment days, and one separately initiated preparation per line each day. Each available condition receives one culture tube; stimulation is common to all tubes, followed by vehicle or R for the same duration. Each lysate is assayed in three multiplex wells measuring five proteins. Thus the three wells are technical measurement repeats, not separately treated biological units. The tube receives treatment; independent biological replication for treatment comparisons comes from preparation/day repeats, with common preparation and day structure retained. Line is not an independent replicate of a universal cell population. No pooling of preparations occurred.

**Conceptual point:** Assignment units, biological replication and technical measurements are different counts.

**Likely misconception:** Three assay wells supply three biological treatment replications.

**Optional follow-up:** At which step was compound R actually applied?

**Facilitation:** Participant reasoning takes priority over instructor explanation. Use these notes selectively; do not read them aloud. This is a fictional teaching scenario, not a published biological finding.
:::

## What else changed when the dose changed? {#r-days .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Trace the day allocation · 1 minute</p>
<img class="data-plot workshop-plot" src="figures/generated/workshop-days.png" alt="Day allocation: both lines have vehicle low medium on day 1, vehicle high on day 2, and all doses on day 3." /><p class="takeaway">How would you allocate the next experiment across days?</p>
<p class="fine">One preparation per line per day; three assay wells per treated tube. Blank = not run.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 02:47–02:48 (1 minute).**

**Say:** Explain that available plate capacity led to vehicle/low/medium on day 1, vehicle/high on day 2, and all conditions on day 3, identically for both lines. Allocation within each day was randomized, and every treated tube has a contemporaneous vehicle. This is an incomplete, imbalanced block design, not perfect treatment/day confounding. Comparing pooled dose means without day structure mixes different day compositions. Some within-day contrasts remain identifiable; only two preparations per line inform each nonzero dose. Day and preparation cannot be separately disentangled within a line here. Ask for balanced complete blocks next time if feasible, with randomized tube and assay positions. A model cannot replace the missing independent replication or create an unobserved condition.

**Conceptual point:** Shared vehicle controls help, but day imbalance still affects what can be compared and how precisely.

**Likely misconception:** Any batch imbalance makes every contrast impossible, or a day covariate cures all design limitations.

**Optional follow-up:** Which comparisons are supported within the same day?

**Facilitation:** Participant reasoning takes priority over instructor explanation. Use these notes selectively; do not read them aloud. This is a fictional teaching scenario, not a published biological finding.
:::

## “Suppresses inflammation”—in what experimental space? {#r-claim .interaction}

<p class=”prompt-tag”>Choose the narrowest defensible claim</p>
<div class=”workshop-claims”><p>These wells</p><p>Future preparations of this line, under these conditions</p><p>Both tested lines</p><p>Cultured cells generally</p><p>Patients</p></div>
<p class="takeaway">Which claim could this design support?</p>

::: notes
**Time: 02:48–02:49 (1 minute).**

**Say:** Ask for a scoped statement. A lower signal for one protein in one cell-line preparation is not proof of broad suppression of inflammation. Comparable future preparations of a stated line under the laboratory protocol are a plausible narrow target for a better replicated follow-up. Two available lines are not a random sample of all cells or patients. The same inflammatory stimulation and matched solvent were used throughout. Vehicle controls solvent and handling under stimulation; it does not establish absence of toxicity or assay interference. If the mechanistic claim requires those distinctions, request suitable viability/assay controls using concepts already taught. Do not add a separate new methods lesson.

**Conceptual point:** Scope follows sampling, endpoints and controls rather than statistical significance.

**Likely misconception:** A significant result determines external validity or mechanism.

**Optional follow-up:** What would need to vary to support the next broader claim?

**Facilitation:** Participant reasoning takes priority over instructor explanation. Use these notes selectively; do not read them aloud. This is a fictional teaching scenario, not a published biological finding.
:::

## How many chances did we give ourselves? {#r-opportunities .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Count before the reveal</p>
<p class="question">2 lines × 3 doses × 5 proteins</p>
<p class="small fragment">30 line–dose–protein comparisons of scientific interest.<br>60 day-specific comparisons were inspected.</p>
<p class="takeaway">Which claims form the family—and what was the purpose?</p>

::: notes
**Time: 02:49–02:50 (1 minute).**

**Say:** Allow a quick response before revealing the actual audit. The researcher compared each available dose with its same-day vehicle separately for every line/protein: two contrasts on day 1, one on day 2 and three on day 3, times two lines times five proteins, giving sixty technical-well Welch calculations. These tests share controls and protein measurements, so they are dependent; neither sixty nor thirty is an effective independent-test count. The .032 panel was selected as a promising example, not a prespecified primary endpoint and not necessarily the minimum p-value. The researcher had a broad exploratory goal and chose the analysis/reporting focus after seeing the screen. Define purpose and family before proposing a multiplicity strategy. Adjustment cannot repair invalid biological replication. Show all outcomes and uncertainty where defensible; do not mechanically calculate .032 times sixty.

**Conceptual point:** Selection and dependence matter beyond a single reported p-value.

**Likely misconception:** Counting tests and adjusting p alone repairs pseudoreplication and selection.

**Optional follow-up:** What would be primary in a confirmatory repeat, and what would remain exploratory?

**Facilitation:** Participant reasoning takes priority over instructor explanation. Use these notes selectively; do not read them aloud. This is a fictional teaching scenario, not a published biological finding.
:::

## “One value was excluded because it looked wrong.” {#r-exclusion .interaction}

<p class="question">What would you need to know?</p>
<p class="small fragment">Line A · day 3 · low dose · protein P3<br>One of three assay-well readings; no recorded failure or prior QC rule.</p>
<p class="fine">The excluded value is not in the p = 0.032 panel.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 02:50–02:51 (1 minute).**

**Say:** Ask for evidence before revealing the location. The value is 190 activity units; the other technical readings are retained. The record does not establish assay failure, recording error or biological cause. No prospective exclusion criterion was documented. The choice was made after viewing the screen, but we do not know whether the researcher checked its influence on a p-value. Do not invent intent. The exclusion is in another protein/line/dose, so it did not generate the selected .032 result. Valid exclusions are possible with a defensible measurement-based reason and audit trail. Retain it for transparent review and report sensitivity if unresolved; do not use a significance-improving rule.

**Conceptual point:** Exclusion needs a reason grounded in measurement or data generation.

**Likely misconception:** Either every extreme value must be deleted or none can ever be excluded.

**Optional follow-up:** What record would turn an unexplained extreme reading into a documented QC failure?

**Facilitation:** Participant reasoning takes priority over instructor explanation. Use these notes selectively; do not read them aloud. This is a fictional teaching scenario, not a published biological finding.
:::

## Describe the data before testing them. {#r-full-data .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Describe what you see · 2 minutes</p>
<img class="data-plot workshop-plot workshop-full" src="figures/generated/workshop-full-data.png" alt="All ninety tube-level protein means, arranged by line and protein, with day traces and the mean containing the excluded reading circled." /><p class="small">Direction · magnitude · variability · consistency</p>
<p class="fine">V/L/M/H = vehicle/low/medium/high. Each point = one tube mean, including all three assay wells.<br>Lines join conditions in the same preparation/day. Open ring: mean containing the excluded reading.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 02:51–02:53 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** Give most of these two minutes to participants. All 90 tube/protein summaries are shown: two lines, nine available condition-tubes per line across days, five proteins. These are not 90 independent biological observations. Conditions on a trace share a preparation; proteins from a lysate and lines on a day share sources of variation. Means include the excluded reading; its marked tube mean is therefore different from the researcher’s retained-well mean. Day traces do not imply longitudinal follow-up or a fitted dose-response curve. Ask about decrease, size on the displayed arbitrary assay scale, variation across days and inconsistent proteins. Signal values across proteins are not directly comparable biological effect scales. P1 tends to decline with dose in this constructed screen, but effect estimates across independent preparations remain uncertain with so few repeats. Avoid significance stars and a new pooled p-value. The individual excluded reading can be checked in the CSV or facilitator figure; the full plot shows biological-unit summaries, not technical rows counted as N.

**Conceptual point:** Raw unit-level views expose variation and selective reporting while preserving dependence.

**Likely misconception:** Every plotted point is independent, or a visual trend proves the broad claim.

**Optional follow-up:** Which comparison appears worth a prospectively specified repeat?

**Facilitation:** Participant reasoning takes priority over instructor explanation. Use these notes selectively; do not read them aloud. This is a fictional teaching scenario, not a published biological finding.
:::

## Repeat the study so it can answer your biological question. {#r-redesign .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Pairs or small groups · 6 minutes · keywords or a sketch are enough</p><div class="workshop-canvas"><p><strong>Question / claim</strong><br>What do we want to learn, and for which experimental space?</p><p><strong>Unit / outcome</strong><br>What receives treatment independently? What will we measure?</p><p><strong>Primary comparison</strong><br>Which effect is the main scientific target?</p><p><strong>Replication</strong><br>Which biological variation must be sampled? Which technical uncertainty controlled?</p><p><strong>Design / allocation</strong><br>Where can pairing or blocking help? How will we randomize and balance days?</p><p><strong>Sample size</strong><br>What relevant effect, plausible variability and precision/power guide N?</p><p><strong>Multiplicity</strong><br>Which outcomes and comparisons are confirmatory or exploratory?</p><p><strong>QC / analysis</strong><br>What rules come first? Which effect, CI and model fit the design?</p></div>

::: notes
**Time: 02:53–02:59 (6 minutes).**

**Say:** Distribute workshop-design-canvas.html as a one-page handout or keep this slide visible. Give six minutes, with a one-minute warning. Participants choose a defensible narrow question and sketch the allocation/replication. They need not fill every box in prose. Circulate and ask what independently repeats, which sources of biological variation matter, whether controls support the claim, how the primary effect is defined, and what sample-size inputs are still missing. Do not provide an invented numerical N without a scientifically relevant effect and plausible variability. Encourage different legitimate questions: one chosen line/protein/dose confirmation versus a broader exploratory screen with an explicit family. Keep participants talking; do not lecture through the canvas.

**Conceptual point:** Prospective question, design and analysis decisions reinforce each other.

**Likely misconception:** There is one correct redesign or a magic independent sample size.

**Optional follow-up:** What would you change if the primary aim were discovery rather than confirmation?

**Facilitation:** Participant reasoning takes priority over instructor explanation. Use these notes selectively; do not read them aloud. This is a fictional teaching scenario, not a published biological finding.
:::

## One defensible repeat—not the only one. {#r-one-redesign}

<div class="workshop-canvas">
<p><strong>Focus</strong><br>Line B · P1 · high R versus vehicle<br>Mean change under the same stimulation protocol</p>
<p><strong>Replicate</strong><br>New independent preparations; both conditions in each preparation</p>
<p><strong>Allocate</strong><br>Balance within day; randomize tube and assay positions</p>
<p><strong>Plan N</strong><br>Relevant effect + biological variability → target precision/power</p>
<p><strong>Separate purposes</strong><br>Primary confirmation; remaining screen explicitly exploratory</p>
<p><strong>Analyse and report</strong><br>Prespecified QC; paired effects and CIs; technical wells retained for precision</p></div>

::: notes
**Time: 02:59–03:02 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Ask one group to describe its choice for a minute before revealing or discussing this example. Then spend two minutes comparing. This independent repeat confirms a hypothesis generated by the original screen; choosing the focus now does not make the old result confirmatory. Prepare multiple independently initiated Line B cultures; split each across vehicle and high R, with same-day matched handling and randomized positions. Retain three assay repeats for precision, average after prospectively defined QC, and analyse independent preparation differences if their assumptions are credible. If multiple preparations share day-dependent treatment effects, balance/block and reflect the dependence; sample days as required by the target. Choose independent N prospectively from a minimum relevant effect, plausible SD of paired differences, desired precision/power, alpha and attrition; no reliable N is determined by this tiny screen. Add controls needed to distinguish reduced protein response from assay interference or nonspecific cell loss before claiming a mechanism. Secondary lines/doses/proteins remain transparently exploratory or receive a prespecified family and suitable multiplicity plan. Report estimates, intervals, raw structure and any p-values.

**Conceptual point:** A defensible repeat depends on the question, not on one universally correct template.

**Likely misconception:** Selecting a primary outcome now validates the earlier selected p-value.

**Optional follow-up:** How would your design change if both cell lines were central to the claim?

**Facilitation:** Participant reasoning takes priority over instructor explanation. Use these notes selectively; do not read them aloud. This is a fictional teaching scenario, not a published biological finding.
:::

## What improved before any test was run? {#r-what-changed .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Name your most consequential change · 1 minute</p>
<div class="research-paths"><div><h3>Original report</h3><p>Broad claim; selected panel<br>n counted assay wells<br>Incomplete day blocks<br>Unrecorded exclusion rationale<br>Analysis chosen after the screen</p></div><div><h3>Prospective repeat</h3><p>Scoped question and primary effect<br>Defined biological replication<br>Balanced, randomized allocation<br>QC and reporting specified<br>N and model follow the design</p></div></div>
<p class="takeaway">Most of the improvement happened before the statistical test.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 03:02–03:04 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** Invite groups to identify their most consequential change and one remaining limitation. Preserve useful features of the original: contemporaneous controls, some day overlap, two lines and a legitimate exploratory screen. Some issues can be improved analytically now: show all data, clarify provenance, restore/review the unexplained exclusion, respect blocks, and label selection. Other limits cannot be repaired from these data: inadequate independent replication, unmeasured controls and restricted experimental space. Explain that a new experiment supplies information, not just a more favourable p-value. Avoid implying the original researcher was incompetent.

**Conceptual point:** Better inference starts with information and prospective design.

**Likely misconception:** Changing the named test is the main improvement.

**Optional follow-up:** Which improvement requires new data rather than a reanalysis?

**Facilitation:** Participant reasoning takes priority over instructor explanation. Use these notes selectively; do not read them aloud. This is a fictional teaching scenario, not a published biological finding.
:::

## “My p-value is 0.032. Is my result real?” {#r-real .interaction}

<p class="question">How would you respond now?</p>
<p class="small fragment">Tell me how the experiment was done, what was independently repeated,<br>what effect you wanted to estimate—and how this result was selected.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 03:04–03:05 (1 minute).**

**Say:** Give participants about forty seconds to formulate a response before revealing the final prompt. Seek a useful conversation rather than yes/no. The laboratory observations exist, but their interpretation depends on design, uncertainty and selection; this technical-well p-value cannot support the biological claim as reported. A promising exploratory pattern can justify an independent repeat without being treated as established truth.

**Conceptual point:** A p-value invites an evidence conversation rather than a binary reality judgment.

**Likely misconception:** Scepticism requires dismissing the data or the researcher.

**Optional follow-up:** What practical next step would you recommend first?

**Facilitation:** Participant reasoning takes priority over instructor explanation. Use these notes selectively; do not read them aloud. This is a fictional teaching scenario, not a published biological finding.
:::

## From a biological question to a defensible claim {#course-whole}

<div class="workshop-surround"><p>Design and analysis decisions surround the whole process</p><div class="workshop-flow">Question → experiment → experimental units → variation<br>→ data → effect estimate → uncertainty<br>→ model → inference → claim</div><p>Power: information needed for the intended effect<br>Multiplicity: opportunities created by the intended claims</p></div>

::: notes
**Time: 03:05–03:06 (1 minute).**

**Say:** Use the diagram as a reconstruction, not another list of definitions. Ask where the group made its most important decision. The path is iterative: a model informs estimation and uncertainty even though it is named later in this conceptual chain; planning revisits the question and design. Power follows the relevant effect and independent information, while multiplicity follows intended claims and selection opportunities. Neither is an isolated last-minute statistical repair. Do not introduce a new formula.

**Conceptual point:** Statistical reasoning links the entire research process.

**Likely misconception:** Design is finished before statistical reasoning begins.

**Optional follow-up:** Where would earlier consultation have changed this experiment most?

**Facilitation:** Participant reasoning takes priority over instructor explanation. Use these notes selectively; do not read them aloud. This is a fictional teaching scenario, not a published biological finding.
:::

## Statistics cannot rescue an experiment that could not answer the question. {#course-landing}

<p class="question">Design the experiment and the analysis together.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 03:06–03:07 (1 minute).**

**Say:** Connect explicitly to the opening motivation: researchers often seek statistical help only after collecting data. This is an invitation to bring the biological question and protocol earlier, not a criticism of colleagues or a claim that imperfect data are worthless. Thoughtful reanalysis may recover supported comparisons; it cannot create missing independent units, identify completely confounded effects or supply absent population coverage. Ask each participant to choose one design conversation to have before the next collection. Thank them and stop here.

**Conceptual point:** Plan the evidence and its interpretation together.

**Likely misconception:** A flawed report means no useful learning or follow-up is possible.

**Optional follow-up:** What will you discuss with a collaborator before the next experiment?

**Facilitation:** Participant reasoning takes priority over instructor explanation. Use these notes selectively; do not read them aloud. This is a fictional teaching scenario, not a published biological finding.
:::
